claim: The SUUR protein inhibits replication fork progression within specific regions of the genome to promote DNA underreplication in Drosophila polyploid cells.
source: In Drosophila polyploid cells, the SNF2-domain-containing SUUR protein inhibits replication fork progression within specific regions of the genome to promote DNA underreplication.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of SUUR.

claim: SUUR interacts with Rif1.
source: While dissecting the function of SUUR's SNF2 domain, we identified an interaction between SUUR and Rif1.
evidence: The abstract states this interaction was identified during the study.

claim: Rif1 regulates the replication timing program.
source: Rif1 has many roles in DNA metabolism and regulates the replication timing program.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about Rif1.

claim: Repression of DNA replication is dependent on Rif1.
source: We demonstrate that repression of DNA replication is dependent on Rif1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Rif1 localizes to active replication forks in a partially SUUR-dependent manner.
source: Rif1 localizes to active replication forks in a partially SUUR-dependent manner and directly regulates replication fork progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Rif1 directly regulates replication fork progression.
source: Rif1 localizes to active replication forks in a partially SUUR-dependent manner and directly regulates replication fork progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: SUUR associates with replication forks in the absence of Rif1.
source: Importantly, SUUR associates with replication forks in the absence of Rif1, indicating that Rif1 acts downstream of SUUR to inhibit fork progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Rif1 acts downstream of SUUR to inhibit fork progression.
source: Importantly, SUUR associates with replication forks in the absence of Rif1, indicating that Rif1 acts downstream of SUUR to inhibit fork progression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data stated in the abstract.

claim: Rif1 protein functions as a regulator of replication fork progression.
source: Our findings uncover an unrecognized function of the Rif1 protein as a regulator of replication fork progression.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Accurate duplication of a cell's genetic information is essential to maintain genome stability.
source: Accurate duplication of a cell's genetic information is essential to maintain genome stability.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Proper regulation of DNA replication is necessary to prevent mutations and other chromosome aberrations that are associated with cancer and developmental abnormalities.
source: Proper regulation of DNA replication is necessary to prevent mutations and other chromosome aberrations that are associated with cancer and developmental abnormalities (Jackson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jackson et al., 2014.

claim: DNA replication begins at thousands of cis-acting sites termed origins of replication.
source: DNA replication begins at thousands of cis-acting sites termed origins of replication.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) binds to replication origins where, together with Cdt1 and Cdc6, it loads an inactive form of the MCM2-7 replicative helicase.
source: The Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) binds to replication origins where, together with Cdt1 and Cdc6, it loads an inactive form of the MCM2-7 replicative helicase (Bell and Labib, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bell and Labib, 2016.

claim: Inactive helicases are phosphorylated by two key kinases, S-CDK and Dbf4-dependent kinase (DDK), which results in the activation of the helicase and recruitment of additional factors to form a pair of bi-directional replication forks emanating outward from the origin of replication.
source: Inactive helicases are phosphorylated by two key kinases, S-CDK and Dbf4-dependent kinase (DDK), which results in the activation of the helicase and recruitment of additional factors to form a pair of bi-directional replication forks emanating outward from the origin of replication (Siddiqui et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Siddiqui et al., 2013.

claim: Much less is known about how replication fork progression is regulated compared to the regulation of DNA replication initiation.
source: Although many layers of regulation control the initiation of DNA replication, much less is known about how replication fork progression is regulated.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: In metazoans, replication origins are not sequence specific and are likely specified by a combination of epigenetic and structural features.
source: In metazoans, replication origins are not sequence specific and are likely specified by a combination of epigenetic and structural features (Aggarwal and Calvi, 2004; Cayrou et al., 2011; Eaton et al., 2011; Mesner et al., 2011; Miotto et al., 2016; Remus et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Replication origins are not uniformly distributed throughout the genome.
source: Furthermore, replication origins are not uniformly distributed throughout the genome.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In origin-poor regions of the genome, a single replication fork must travel great distances to complete replication.
source: The result of non-uniform origin distribution is that, in origin-poor regions of the genome, a single replication fork must travel great distances to complete replication.
evidence: This is a logical inference from non-uniform origin distribution.

claim: If a replication fork encounters an impediment within a large origin-less region of the genome, then replication will be incomplete, resulting in genome instability.
source: If a replication fork encounters an impediment within a large origin-less region of the genome, then replication will be incomplete, resulting in genome instability (Newman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Newman et al., 2013.

claim: Origin-poor regions of the genome are associated with chromosome fragility and genome instability.
source: In fact, origin-poor regions of the genome are known to be associated with chromosome fragility and genome instability (Debatisse et al., 2012; Durkin and Glover, 2007; Letessier et al., 2011; Norio et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is a need to regulate both the initiation and elongation phases of DNA replication to maintain genome stability.
source: This highlights the need to regulate both the initiation and elongation phases of DNA replication to maintain genome stability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the previous statements about origin-poor regions.

claim: DNA replication is regulated in a temporal manner where specific DNA sequences replicate at precise times during S phase, a process known as the DNA replication timing program.
source: DNA replication is also regulated in a temporal manner where specific DNA sequences replicate at precise times during S phase, a process known as the DNA replication timing program.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Euchromatin replicates in the early part of S phase.
source: While euchromatin replicates in the early part of S phase, heterochromatin and other repressive chromatin types replicate in the latter portion of S phase (Gilbert, 2002; Rhind and Gilbert, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gilbert, 2002 and Rhind and Gilbert, 2013.

claim: Heterochromatin and other repressive chromatin types replicate in the latter portion of S phase.
source: While euchromatin replicates in the early part of S phase, heterochromatin and other repressive chromatin types replicate in the latter portion of S phase (Gilbert, 2002; Rhind and Gilbert, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gilbert, 2002 and Rhind and Gilbert, 2013.

claim: The underlying molecular mechanisms controlling replication timing have remained elusive.
source: Although the process of replication timing has been appreciated for many years, the underlying molecular mechanisms controlling timing have remained elusive.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Replication timing is an actively regulated process.
source: The discovery of factors that regulate the DNA replication timing program, however, demonstrate that replication timing is an actively regulated process.
evidence: This is an inference from the discovery of regulatory factors.

claim: Rif1 (Rap1-interacting factor 1) regulates replication timing from yeast to humans.
source: One factor that regulates replication timing from yeast to humans is Rif1 (Rap1-interacting factor 1).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Rif1 was initially identified as a regulator of telomere length in budding yeast.
source: Rif1 was initially identified as a regulator of telomere length in budding yeast (Hardy et al., 1992), but this function of Rif1 appears to be specific to yeast (Xu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hardy et al., 1992 and Xu et al., 2004.

claim: The telomere length regulation function of Rif1 appears to be specific to yeast.
source: Rif1 was initially identified as a regulator of telomere length in budding yeast (Hardy et al., 1992), but this function of Rif1 appears to be specific to yeast (Xu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2004.

claim: Rif1 has been shown to regulate multiple aspects of DNA replication and repair.
source: Subsequently, Rif1 has been shown to regulate multiple aspects of DNA replication and repair.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In mammalian cells, Rif1 regulates DNA repair pathway choice by preventing resection of double-strand breaks and favoring non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) over homologous recombination.
source: In mammalian cells, Rif1 has been shown to regulate DNA repair pathway choice by preventing resection of double-strand breaks and favoring non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) over homologous recombination (Chapman et al., 2013; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Zimmermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chapman et al., 2013; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Zimmermann et al., 2013.

claim: Rif1 from multiple organisms contains a Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1) interaction motif.
source: Rif1 from multiple organisms contains a Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1) interaction motif and Rif1 is able to recruit PP1 to DDK-activated helicases to inactive them and prevent initiation of replication (Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2017.

claim: Rif1 is able to recruit PP1 to DDK-activated helicases to inactivate them and prevent initiation of replication.
source: Rif1 from multiple organisms contains a Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1) interaction motif and Rif1 is able to recruit PP1 to DDK-activated helicases to inactive them and prevent initiation of replication (Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2017.

claim: In yeasts, flies and mammalian cells, Rif1 has been shown to regulate the replication timing program.
source: In yeasts, flies and mammalian cells, Rif1 has been shown to regulate the replication timing program (Cornacchia et al., 2012; Hayano et al., 2012; Peace et al., 2014; Sreesankar et al., 2015; Yamazaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The precise mechanism(s) through which Rif1 functions to control replication timing are not fully understood.
source: The precise mechanism(s) through which Rif1 functions to control replication timing are not fully understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Rif1 has been shown to interact with Lamin and is thought to tether specific regions of the genome to the nuclear periphery.
source: For example, Rif1 has been show to interact with Lamin and is thought to tether specific regions of the genome to the nuclear periphery (Foti et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Foti et al., 2016.

claim: How Rif1's activity of tethering genome regions to the nuclear periphery is related to Rif1's ability to inactivate helicases together with PP1 in controlling the timing program remains obscure.
source: How this activity is related to Rif1's ability to inactivate helicases together with PP1 in controlling the timing program remains obscure.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Studying DNA replication in the context of development provides a powerful method to understand how DNA replication is regulated both spatially and temporally.
source: Studying DNA replication in the context of development provides a powerful method to understand how DNA replication is regulated both spatially and temporally.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale in the introduction.

claim: DNA replication must be flexible enough to accommodate the changes in S phase length and cell cycle parameters that occur as cells differentiate.
source: Although DNA replication is a highly ordered process, it must be flexible enough to accommodate the changes in S phase length and cell cycle parameters that occur as cells differentiate (Matson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Matson et al., 2017.

claim: During Drosophila development the length of S phase can vary from ~8 hr in a differentiated mitotic cell to 3 – 4 min during early embryonic cell cycles.
source: For example, during Drosophila development the length of S phase can vary from ~8 hr in a differentiated mitotic cell to 3 – 4 min during early embryonic cell cycles (Blumenthal et al., 1974; Spradling and Orr-Weaver, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blumenthal et al., 1974 and Spradling and Orr-Weaver, 1987.

claim: Many tissues and cell types in Drosophila are polyploid, having multiple copies of the genome in a single cell.
source: Additionally, many tissues and cell types in Drosophila are polyploid, having multiple copies of the genome in a single cell (Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001; Lilly and Duronio, 2005; Zielke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001; Lilly and Duronio, 2005; Zielke et al., 2013.

claim: In polyploid cells, copy number is not always uniform throughout the genome.
source: In polyploid cells, copy number is not always uniform throughout the genome (Rudkin, 1969; Hua and Orr-Weaver, 2017; Spradling and Orr-Weaver, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rudkin, 1969; Hua and Orr-Weaver, 2017; Spradling and Orr-Weaver, 1987.

claim: Both heterochromatin and several euchromatic regions of the genome have reduced DNA copy number relative to overall ploidy.
source: Both heterochromatin and several euchromatic regions of the genome have reduced DNA copy number relative to overall ploidy (Nordman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nordman et al., 2011.

claim: Underreplicated euchromatic regions of the genome share key features with common fragile sites in that they are devoid of replication origins, late replicating, display DNA damage and are tissue-specific.
source: Underreplicated euchromatic regions of the genome share key features with common fragile sites in that they are devoid of replication origins, late replicating, display DNA damage and are tissue-specific (Andreyeva et al., 2008; Nordman et al., 2014; Sher et al., 2012; Yarosh and Spradling, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Andreyeva et al., 2008; Nordman et al., 2014; Sher et al., 2012; Yarosh and Spradling, 2014.

claim: The presence of underreplication is conserved in mammalian cells.
source: The presence of underreplication is conserved in mammalian cells, but the mechanism(s) mammalian cells use to promote underreplication is unknown (Hannibal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hannibal et al., 2014.

claim: The mechanism(s) mammalian cells use to promote underreplication is unknown.
source: The presence of underreplication is conserved in mammalian cells, but the mechanism(s) mammalian cells use to promote underreplication is unknown (Hannibal et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap, supported by a citation to Hannibal et al., 2014.

claim: In Drosophila, underreplication is an active process that is largely dependent on the distribution of ORC and on the Suppressor of Underreplication protein, SUUR.
source: In Drosophila, underreplication is an active process that is largely dependent on the distribution of ORC and on the Suppressor of Underreplication protein, SUUR (Hua et al., 2018; Makunin et al., 2002; Nordman and Orr-Weaver, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hua et al., 2018; Makunin et al., 2002; Nordman and Orr-Weaver, 2015.

claim: Understanding how the SUUR protein functions will significantly increase our understanding of the developmental control of DNA replication.
source: Understanding how the SUUR protein functions will significantly increase our understanding of the developmental control of DNA replication.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale in the introduction.

claim: The SUUR protein has a recognizable SNF2-like chromatin remodeling domain at its N-terminus.
source: The SUUR protein has a recognizable SNF2-like chromatin remodeling domain at its N-terminus, but based on sequence analysis, this domain is predicted to be defective for ATP binding and hydrolysis (Makunin et al., 2002; Nordman and Orr-Weaver, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Makunin et al., 2002 and Nordman and Orr-Weaver, 2015.

claim: Based on sequence analysis, SUUR's SNF2 domain is predicted to be defective for ATP binding and hydrolysis.
source: The SUUR protein has a recognizable SNF2-like chromatin remodeling domain at its N-terminus, but based on sequence analysis, this domain is predicted to be defective for ATP binding and hydrolysis (Makunin et al., 2002; Nordman and Orr-Weaver, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Makunin et al., 2002 and Nordman and Orr-Weaver, 2015.

claim: Outside of the SNF2 domain, SUUR has no recognizable motifs or domains.
source: Outside of the SNF2 domain, SUUR has no recognizable motifs or domains, which has hampered a mechanistic understanding of how SUUR promotes underreplication.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: SUUR was shown to control copy number by directly reducing replication fork progression.
source: Recently, however, SUUR was shown to control copy number by directly reducing replication fork progression (Nordman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nordman et al., 2014.

claim: SUUR associates with active replication forks.
source: SUUR associates with active replication forks and while loss of SUUR function results in increased replication fork progression, overexpression of SUUR drastically inhibits fork progression without affecting origin firing (Nordman et al., 2014; Sher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nordman et al., 2014 and Sher et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of SUUR function results in increased replication fork progression.
source: SUUR associates with active replication forks and while loss of SUUR function results in increased replication fork progression, overexpression of SUUR drastically inhibits fork progression without affecting origin firing (Nordman et al., 2014; Sher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nordman et al., 2014 and Sher et al., 2012.

claim: Overexpression of SUUR drastically inhibits fork progression without affecting origin firing.
source: SUUR associates with active replication forks and while loss of SUUR function results in increased replication fork progression, overexpression of SUUR drastically inhibits fork progression without affecting origin firing (Nordman et al., 2014; Sher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nordman et al., 2014 and Sher et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of SUUR function has no influence on ORC binding.
source: These findings, together with previous work showing that loss of SUUR function has no influence on ORC binding (Sher et al., 2012) and that SUUR associates with euchromatin in an S phase-dependent manner (Kolesnikova et al., 2013), further supports SUUR as a direct inhibitor of replication fork progression within specific regions of the genome.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sher et al., 2012.

claim: SUUR associates with euchromatin in an S phase-dependent manner.
source: These findings, together with previous work showing that loss of SUUR function has no influence on ORC binding (Sher et al., 2012) and that SUUR associates with euchromatin in an S phase-dependent manner (Kolesnikova et al., 2013), further supports SUUR as a direct inhibitor of replication fork progression within specific regions of the genome.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kolesnikova et al., 2013.

claim: SUUR is a direct inhibitor of replication fork progression within specific regions of the genome.
source: These findings, together with previous work showing that loss of SUUR function has no influence on ORC binding (Sher et al., 2012) and that SUUR associates with euchromatin in an S phase-dependent manner (Kolesnikova et al., 2013), further supports SUUR as a direct inhibitor of replication fork progression within specific regions of the genome.
evidence: This is an inference from multiple cited studies.

claim: The mechanism through which SUUR is recruited to replication forks and how it inhibits their progression remains poorly understood.
source: The mechanism through which SUUR is recruited to replication forks and how it inhibits their progression remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Localization of SUUR to replication forks, but not heterochromatin, is dependent on its SNF2 domain.
source: We show that localization of SUUR to replication forks, but not heterochromatin, is dependent on its SNF2 domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction.

claim: Underreplication is dependent on Rif1.
source: Importantly, we demonstrate that underreplication is dependent on Rif1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction.

claim: Rif1 acts downstream of SUUR to control replication fork progression.
source: Critically, we have shown that Rif1 localizes to replication forks in an SUUR-dependent manner, where it acts downstream of SUUR to control replication fork progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction.

claim: The findings provide mechanistic insight into the process of underreplication.
source: Our findings provide mechanistic insight into the process of underreplication and define a new function for Rif1 in replication control.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the introduction.

claim: The findings define a new function for Rif1 in replication control.
source: Our findings provide mechanistic insight into the process of underreplication and define a new function for Rif1 in replication control.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the introduction.

claim: The SNF2 domain of SUUR is essential for SUUR function.
source: The effect of deleting the SNF2 domain was qualitatively and quantitatively similar to the SuUR null mutant.
evidence: This is based on comparison of copy number profiles between SuURΔSNF and SuUR null mutants.

claim: Out of the 90 underreplicated sites identified in WT salivary glands, 59 were not detected in the SuUR∆SNF mutant.
source: Quantitatively, out of the 90 underreplicated sites identified in WT salivary glands, 59 were not detected in the SuUR∆SNF mutant (Supplementary file 1) and copy number was significantly increased in the euchromatic underreplicated domains similar to the SuUR null mutant (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study.

claim: Copy number was significantly increased in the euchromatic underreplicated domains in the SuUR∆SNF mutant similar to the SuUR null mutant.
source: Quantitatively, out of the 90 underreplicated sites identified in WT salivary glands, 59 were not detected in the SuUR∆SNF mutant (Supplementary file 1) and copy number was significantly increased in the euchromatic underreplicated domains similar to the SuUR null mutant (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The SNF2-like domain of SUUR is necessary to promote underreplication.
source: Our findings show that the SNF2-like domain of SUUR is necessary to promote underreplication.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the SuURΔSNF mutant analysis.

claim: SUUR localizes to both replication forks and heterochromatin in amplifying follicle cells.
source: In agreement with previous studies, SUUR localized to both replication forks and heterochromatin in amplifying follicle cells (Figure 1E) (Nordman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and a citation to Nordman et al., 2014.

claim: The SUUR∆SNF mutant localized to heterochromatin, but its recruitment to active replication forks was severely reduced.
source: In contrast, the SUUR∆SNF mutant localized to heterochromatin, but its recruitment to active replication forks was severely reduced (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The SNF2 domain is important for SUUR recruitment to replication forks.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that the SNF2 domain is important for SUUR recruitment to replication forks and is essential for SUUR-mediated underreplication.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the localization and functional studies of SuURΔSNF.

claim: The SNF2 domain is essential for SUUR-mediated underreplication.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that the SNF2 domain is important for SUUR recruitment to replication forks and is essential for SUUR-mediated underreplication.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the localization and functional studies of SuURΔSNF.

claim: Overexpression of the C-terminal two-thirds of SUUR promotes underreplication.
source: Whereas overexpression of the C-terminal two-thirds of SUUR promotes underreplication (Kolesnikova et al., 2005), overexpression of the SNF2 domain suppresses underreplication in the presence of endogenous SUUR (Kolesnikova et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kolesnikova et al., 2005.

claim: Overexpression of the SNF2 domain suppresses underreplication in the presence of endogenous SUUR.
source: Whereas overexpression of the C-terminal two-thirds of SUUR promotes underreplication (Kolesnikova et al., 2005), overexpression of the SNF2 domain suppresses underreplication in the presence of endogenous SUUR (Kolesnikova et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kolesnikova et al., 2005.

claim: The C-terminal region of SUUR has no detectable homology or conserved domains.
source: The C-terminal region of SUUR, however, has no detectable homology or conserved domains (Makunin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Makunin et al., 2002.

claim: SUUR is recruited to replication forks through its SNF2 domain where it could recruit an additional factor(s) through its C-terminus to inhibit replication fork progression.
source: These observations, together with our own results demonstrating that the SNF2 domain of SUUR is responsible for its localization to replication forks, led us to hypothesize that SUUR is recruited to replication forks through its SNF2 domain where it could recruit an additional factor(s) through its C-terminus to inhibit replication fork progression.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data and previous observations.

claim: A single protein fulfilled the criteria of being present only in full-length SUUR purifications and not in the SNF2 domain purification: Rif1.
source: If SUUR recruits a factor to replication forks outside of its SNF2 domain, then we would expect this factor to be present only in full-length purifications and not in the SNF2 domain purification. A single protein fulfilled this criteria: Rif1 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A from IP-mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: Rif1 works together with SUUR to inhibit replication fork progression.
source: This result raises the possibility Rif1 works together with SUUR to inhibit replication fork progression.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the interaction data.

claim: The association between SUUR and Rif1 is not bridged by chromatin.
source: Even in these conditions, SUUR was able to co-IP Rif1 (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). We conclude that SUUR and Rif1 exist in the same protein complex and the interaction between SUUR and Rif1 is independent of chromatin bridging.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP experiments with Benzonase treatment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SUUR and Rif1 exist in the same protein complex.
source: Even in these conditions, SUUR was able to co-IP Rif1 (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). We conclude that SUUR and Rif1 exist in the same protein complex and the interaction between SUUR and Rif1 is independent of chromatin bridging.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the co-IP experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The interaction between SUUR and Rif1 is independent of chromatin bridging.
source: Even in these conditions, SUUR was able to co-IP Rif1 (Figure 2B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). We conclude that SUUR and Rif1 exist in the same protein complex and the interaction between SUUR and Rif1 is independent of chromatin bridging.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the co-IP experiments with Benzonase treatment shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Rif11/Rif12 null mutant was viable and fertile showing only a modest defect in embryonic hatch rate relative to wild-type flies.
source: The Rif11/Rif12 null mutant was viable and fertile showing only a modest defect in embryonic hatch rate relative to wild-type flies with a 92% hatch rate for wild-type embryos vs. 88% for the Rif11/Rif2 mutant embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: A previous study reported Rif1 is essential in Drosophila based on RNAi experiments.
source: This is in contrast to a previous study reporting Rif1 is essential in Drosophila (Sreesankar et al., 2015) and consistent with a recent study that generated an independent Rif1 null mutant using CRISPR-based mutagenesis (Seller and O'Farrell, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sreesankar et al., 2015.

claim: A recent study generated an independent Rif1 null mutant using CRISPR-based mutagenesis that is viable.
source: This is in contrast to a previous study reporting Rif1 is essential in Drosophila (Sreesankar et al., 2015) and consistent with a recent study that generated an independent Rif1 null mutant using CRISPR-based mutagenesis (Seller and O'Farrell, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seller and O'Farrell, 2018.

claim: The lethality in the RNAi experiments was likely due to an off-target effect.
source: Rif1's essentiality, however, was based on RNAi and not a mutation of the Rif1 gene (Sreesankar et al., 2015). The most likely explanation for this discrepancy is that the lethality in the RNAi experiments was due to an off-target effect.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the discrepancy between RNAi and null mutant results.

claim: Underreplication is abolished upon loss of Rif1 function.
source: Strikingly, underreplication is abolished upon loss of Rif1 function (Figure 3B and C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Rif1 is essential for underreplication.
source: Furthermore, we determined the read density at all euchromatic sites of underreplication called in our wild-type samples, which quantitatively demonstrates that Rif1 is essential for underreplication (Figure 3C). These results demonstrate that underreplication is dependent on Rif1.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Rif1 mutants have a clear pattern of late replication in endo cycling cells.
source: Therefore, we conclude that Rif1 mutants still have a clear pattern of late replication.
evidence: This is based on EdU incorporation patterns in heterochromatin shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Replication timing cannot solely explain the lack of underreplication associated with loss of Rif1 function.
source: Given that heterochromatin underreplication is suppressed in a Rif1 mutant, although it is still late replicating, indicates that replication timing cannot solely explain the lack of underreplication associated with loss of Rif1 function.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that Rif1 mutants maintain late replication but lack underreplication.

claim: The chromocenters were abnormally large in the Rif1 mutant relative to an SuUR mutant as observed by DAPI staining.
source: First, although underreplication is suppressed in both mutants (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the chromocenters were abnormally large in the Rif1 mutant relative to an SuUR mutant as observed by DAPI staining consistent with the 'fluffy' enlarged chromocenters seen in Rif1 mutant mouse cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) (Cornacchia et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and a citation to Cornacchia et al., 2012.

claim: Illumina-based copy number profiles revealed an increase in copy number in some pericentric heterochromatin regions in the Rif1 mutant relative to the SuUR mutant.
source: Second, Illumina-based copy number profiles revealed an increase in copy number in some pericentric heterochromatin regions in the Rif1 mutant relative to the SuUR mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Heterochromatin is partially, but not fully replicated in SuUR mutant endo cycling cells.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that heterochromatin is partially, but not fully replicated in SuUR mutant endo cycling cells, consistent with previous cytological analysis (Demakova et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by a citation to Demakova et al., 2007.

claim: Loss of Rif1 function appears to completely restore heterochromatic replication in endo cycling cells.
source: In contrast, loss of Rif1 function appears to completely restore heterochromatic replication in endo cycling cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the copy number data in Rif1 mutants.

claim: SUUR-mediated underreplication occurs through inhibition of replication fork progression.
source: SUUR-mediated underreplication occurs through inhibition of replication fork progression (Nordman et al., 2014; Sher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nordman et al., 2014 and Sher et al., 2012.

claim: If SUUR acts together with Rif1 to promote underreplication, then Rif1 is expected to control replication fork progression.
source: If SUUR acts together with Rif1 to promote underreplication, then Rif1 is expected to control replication fork progression.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the hypothesis that SUUR and Rif1 work together.

claim: DNA combing assays in human and mouse cells from multiple groups have come to different conclusions as to whether Rif1 affects replication fork progression.
source: DNA combing assays in human and mouse cells from multiple groups have come to different conclusions as to whether Rif1 affects replication fork progression (Alver et al., 2017; Cornacchia et al., 2012; Hiraga et al., 2017; Yamazaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Rif1 has been shown to be associated with replication forks through nascent chromatin capture.
source: Rif1, however, has been shown to be associated with replication forks through nascent chromatin capture, an iPOND-like technique used to isolate proteins associated with active replication forks (Alabert et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alabert et al., 2014.

claim: Loss of Rif1 function resulted in an increase in replication fork progression without significantly affecting copy number at the origin of replication at all sites of amplification.
source: Loss of Rif1 function resulted in an increase in replication fork progression without significantly affecting copy number at the origin of replication at all sites of amplification (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The increase in fork progression observed in the Rif1 mutant was not due to a lengthening of the developmental time window for gene amplification.
source: The increase in fork progression observed in the Rif1 mutant was not due to a lengthening of the developmental time window for gene amplification, as there was no significant difference in egg chamber distribution between wild-type and Rif1 mutant ovaries (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Origin firing was not affected in the Rif1 mutant.
source: This quantitative analysis of origin firing and replication fork progression revealed that origin firing was not affected in the Rif1 mutant, as no major change in copy number was detected at the origin of replication when comparing wild type and Rif1 mutant stage 13 follicle cells (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The width of each replication gradient was significantly increased at all sites of amplification in the Rif1 mutant.
source: In contrast, the width of each replication gradient, which represents the rate of fork progression, was significantly increased at all sites of amplification (Figure 4A; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Rif1 regulates replication fork progression.
source: Based on the observation that the Rif1 mutant does not affect origin firing, but specifically affects the distance replication forks travel during the gene amplification process, and there was no change in the developmental window of gene amplification in the Rif1 mutant, we conclude that Rif1 regulates replication fork progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the amplification analysis.

claim: A prolonged period of EdU incorporation in the SuUR mutant gives rise to the extended replication gradient at sites of amplification.
source: Previously, it was shown that a prolonged period of EdU incorporation in the SuUR mutant, within the 7.5 hr span of gene amplification, gives rise to the extended replication gradient at sites of amplification (Nordman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nordman et al., 2014.

claim: Loss of Rif1 function resulted in a prolonged period of EdU incorporation with 98.5% of stage 13 follicle cells visibly incorporating EdU compared to 34% in wild-type.
source: Similar to an SuUR mutant, loss of Rif1 function also resulted in a prolonged period of EdU incorporation with 34% of follicle cells visibly incorporating EdU in wild-type follicle cells, 100% in an SuUR mutant and 98.5% in the Rif1 mutant (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Rif1 has a destabilizing effect on replication forks, resulting in a premature cessation of replication fork progression.
source: This result suggests that Rif1 has a destabilizing effect on replication forks, resulting in a premature cessation of replication fork progression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EdU incorporation data.

claim: SUUR localized to both replication forks and heterochromatin in the absence of Rif1 function.
source: SUUR localized to both replication forks and heterochromatin in the absence of Rif1 function (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Therefore, we conclude that Rif1 acts downstream of SUUR to inhibit fork progression and that SUUR lacks the ability to inhibit replication fork progression in the absence of Rif1.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: SUUR lacks the ability to inhibit replication fork progression in the absence of Rif1.
source: SUUR localized to both replication forks and heterochromatin in the absence of Rif1 function (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Therefore, we conclude that Rif1 acts downstream of SUUR to inhibit fork progression and that SUUR lacks the ability to inhibit replication fork progression in the absence of Rif1.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the localization data in Rif1 mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: Rif1 localization pattern was strikingly similar to that of SUUR.
source: Rif1 localization pattern was strikingly similar to that of SUUR.
evidence: This is an observation from the localization studies.

claim: Rif1 is localized to heterochromatin in all stages of amplifying follicle cells.
source: First, Rif1 is localized to heterochromatin in all stages of amplifying follicle cells (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Rif1 localized to sites of amplification even prior to the formation of double bar structures.
source: Second, Rif1 localized to sites of amplification even prior to the formation of double bar structures (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the later stages of gene amplification Rif1 was localized to active replication forks.
source: Third, in the later stages of gene amplification Rif1 was localized to active replication forks.
evidence: This is an observation from the localization studies shown in Figure 6.

claim: Rif1 dynamically associates with replication forks to regulate their progression.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that Rif1 dynamically associates with replication forks to regulate their progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the localization studies.

claim: Rif1 was enriched in EdU pulse samples relative to chase samples in cultured cells.
source: Consistent with Rif1 association with replication forks in amplifying follicle cells, Rif1 was enriched in EdU pulse samples relative to chase samples in cultured cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by iPOND mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Rif1 is associated with replication forks in amplifying follicle cells and cultured cells.
source: Together, these results indicate that Rif1 is associated with replication forks in amplifying follicle cells and cultured cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the iPOND and PLA experiments.

claim: Rif1's association with replication forks was largely dependent on SUUR.
source: We found that Rif1's association with replication forks was largely dependent on SUUR, as the Rif1 signal was lost in late stage amplifying follicle cells in an SuUR mutant (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The initial recruitment of Rif1 to sites of amplification is not completely dependent on SUUR.
source: Rif1's recruitment to replication foci, however, was not completely dependent on SUUR. In a subset of stage 10B and 11 egg chambers, when both initiation of replication and fork progression are still coupled, we observed Rif1 localization to amplification foci in a subset of follicle cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: SUUR is necessary to retain Rif1 at replication forks.
source: We conclude that while the initial recruitment of Rif1 to sites of amplification is not completely dependent on SUUR, SUUR is necessary to retain Rif1 at replication forks.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the localization studies in SuUR mutants.

claim: Rif1 associates with Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1) through a conserved interaction motif.
source: Rif1 associates with Protein Phosphatase 1 (PP1) through a conserved interaction motif, thereby recruiting PP1 to MCM complexes and inactivating them (Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2017; Hiraga et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2017; Hiraga et al., 2014.

claim: PP1 has been shown to associate with Rif1 in Drosophila.
source: PP1 has also been shown to associate with Rif1 in Drosophila (Seller and O'Farrell, 2018; Sreesankar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Seller and O'Farrell, 2018 and Sreesankar et al., 2015.

claim: DDK-phosphorylated MCM subunits were shown to be necessary to maintain CMG association and stability of the helicase.
source: More recently, however, DDK-phosphorylated MCM subunits were shown to be necessary to maintain CMG association and stability of the helicase (Alver et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alver et al., 2017.

claim: Continued phosphorylation of the helicase is necessary for replication fork progression.
source: This result suggests that continued phosphorylation of the helicase is necessary for replication fork progression (Alver et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference from the cited study, supported by a citation to Alver et al., 2017.

claim: Mutation of the SILK/RSVF motif has been shown to disrupt the Rif1/PP1 interaction in organisms from yeast to humans.
source: Mutation of this motif has been shown to disrupt the Rif1/PP1 interaction in organisms from yeast to humans (Alver et al., 2017; Davé et al., 2014; Hiraga et al., 2017; Hiraga et al., 2014; Mattarocci et al., 2014; Sreesankar et al., 2015; Sukackaite et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Underreplication was largely abolished in the Rif1PP1 mutant.
source: Similar to the Rif1 mutant, underreplication was largely abolished in the Rif1PP1 mutant (Figure 7A–C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Rif1's PP1-interaction motif is necessary to promote underreplication.
source: Thus, Rif1's PP1-interaction motif is necessary to promote underreplication, suggesting that PP1 is a mediator of underreplication.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the Rif1PP1 mutant analysis.

claim: PP1 is a mediator of underreplication.
source: Thus, Rif1's PP1-interaction motif is necessary to promote underreplication, suggesting that PP1 is a mediator of underreplication.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the Rif1PP1 mutant data.

claim: It remains possible that an additional protein(s) could interact with the PP1-interaction motif to promote underreplication.
source: It still remains possible, however, that an additional protein(s) could interact with this motif to promote underreplication.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative possibility.

claim: SUUR serves as a scaffold to recruit a Rif1/PP1 complex to replication forks where Rif1/PP1 inhibits replication fork progression through dephosphorylation of a component of the replisome.
source: We propose that SUUR recruits Rif1/PP1 to replication forks where it is able to dephosphorylate MCM subunits, ultimately inhibiting replication fork progression.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the study's findings.

claim: The SNF2 domain of SUUR is critical for its ability to localize to replication forks.
source: Our work suggests that the SNF2 domain of SUUR is critical for its ability to localize to replication forks.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the SuURΔSNF localization studies.

claim: SUUR has two distinct modes of chromatin association during the endo cycle: it constitutively localizes to heterochromatin and dynamically associates with replication forks.
source: SUUR has previously been shown to dynamically localize to replication forks during S phase, but constitutively binds to heterochromatin (Kolesnikova et al., 2013; Nordman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kolesnikova et al., 2013 and Nordman et al., 2014.

claim: SUUR associates with HP1 and this interaction occurs between the central region of SUUR and HP1.
source: SUUR associates with HP1 and this interaction occurs between the central region of SUUR and HP1 (Pindyurin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pindyurin et al., 2008.

claim: The interaction between SUUR and HP1 is responsible for constitutive SUUR localization to heterochromatin.
source: Therefore, we speculate that the interaction between SUUR and HP1 is responsible for constitutive SUUR localization to heterochromatin, while a different interaction between the SNF2 domain and a yet to be defined component of the replisome, or replication fork structure itself, recruits SUUR to active replication forks during S phase.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data.

claim: A different interaction between the SNF2 domain and a yet to be defined component of the replisome, or replication fork structure itself, recruits SUUR to active replication forks during S phase.
source: Therefore, we speculate that the interaction between SUUR and HP1 is responsible for constitutive SUUR localization to heterochromatin, while a different interaction between the SNF2 domain and a yet to be defined component of the replisome, or replication fork structure itself, recruits SUUR to active replication forks during S phase.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data.

claim: Overexpression of the SNF2 domain interferes with recruitment of full-length SUUR to replication forks, by saturating potential SUUR binding sites at the replication fork.
source: Together with the data presented here, we suggest that overexpression of the SNF2 domain interferes with recruitment of full-length SUUR to replication forks, by saturating potential SUUR binding sites at the replication fork.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain previous observations.

claim: At physiological levels, the affinity of SUUR for replication forks is substantially diminished in the absence of the SNF2 domain.
source: Although the C-terminal region of SUUR is necessary to induce underreplication (Kolesnikova et al., 2005), the C-terminal portion of SUUR remains associated with heterochromatin in the SUURΔSNF construct, but this protein is not sufficient to induce underreplication. We suggest that at physiological levels, the affinity of SUUR for replication forks is substantially diminished in the absence of the SNF2 domain.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data.

claim: There are several sites that display a modest degree of underreplication in the absence of SUUR.
source: Although underreplication is largely dependent on SUUR, there are several sites that display a modest degree of underreplication in the absence of SUUR (Demakova et al., 2007; Sher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Demakova et al., 2007 and Sher et al., 2012.

claim: In a Rif1 mutant, sites that display modest underreplication in the absence of SUUR are fully replicated and there is no longer any detectable levels of underreplication within any regions of the genome.
source: In a Rif1 mutant, however, these sites are fully replicated and there is no longer any detectable levels of underreplication within any regions of the genome.
evidence: This is based on the copy number data from Rif1 mutants.

claim: Rif1 is capable of promoting underreplication through a mechanism independent of SUUR.
source: It is possible that Rif1 is capable of promoting underreplication through a mechanism independent of SUUR.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility based on the data.

claim: Rif1 is a critical factor in driving underreplication.
source: Therefore, we conclude that Rif1 is a critical factor in driving underreplication.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the Rif1 mutant analysis.

claim: Rif1 controls replication timing in Drosophila and is necessary for the onset of late replication at the mid-blastula transition.
source: While Rif1 controls replication timing in Drosophila and is necessary for the onset of late replication at the mid-blastula transition (Seller and O'Farrell, 2018), we argue that the changes in copy number associated with loss of Rif1 function are not solely due to a loss of late replication.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seller and O'Farrell, 2018.

claim: The changes in copy number associated with loss of Rif1 function are not solely due to a loss of late replication.
source: While Rif1 controls replication timing in Drosophila and is necessary for the onset of late replication at the mid-blastula transition (Seller and O'Farrell, 2018), we argue that the changes in copy number associated with loss of Rif1 function are not solely due to a loss of late replication.
evidence: This is an argument based on the observation that Rif1 mutants maintain late replication patterns.

claim: Previous work in mammalian polyploid cells has shown that underreplication is dependent on Rif1, which was attributed to changes in replication timing.
source: Previous work in mammalian polyploid cells has shown that underreplication is dependent on Rif1, which was attributed to changes in replication timing (Hannibal and Baker, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hannibal and Baker, 2016.

claim: Rif1 may have a direct role in mammalian underreplication through a mechanism similar to that of Drosophila and may not simply be due to indirect changes in replication timing.
source: Our work raises the possibility that Rif1 has a direct role in mammalian underreplication through a mechanism similar to that of Drosophila and may not simply be due to indirect changes in replication timing.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in Drosophila.

claim: The analysis of amplification loci demonstrates that Rif1 controls replication fork progression independently of initiation control.
source: Our analysis of amplification loci demonstrates that Rif1 controls replication fork progression independently of initiation control, thus demonstrating that Rif1 has a specific effect on replication fork progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the amplification analysis.

claim: A new role for Rif1 in DNA metabolism as a regulator of replication fork progression and copy number control has been uncovered.
source: Therefore, we have uncovered a new role for Rif1 in DNA metabolism as a regulator of replication fork progression and copy number control.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.

claim: Rif1 has been identified as part of the replisome in human cells by nascent chromatin capture.
source: Rif1 has been identified as part of the replisome in human cells by nascent chromatin capture, a technique that identifies proteins associated with newly synthesized chromatin (Alabert et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Alabert et al., 2014.

claim: Multiple studies have assessed whether loss of Rif1 function affects replication fork progression in yeast, mouse and human cells, but have come to different conclusions.
source: Multiple studies have assessed whether loss of Rif1 function affects replication fork progression in yeast, mouse and human cells, but have come to different conclusions (Alver et al., 2017; Cornacchia et al., 2012; Hiraga et al., 2017; Yamazaki et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Nearly all DNA fiber assay studies have shown that Rif1 mutants have a slight increase in replication fork progression, although not always statistically significant.
source: DNA fiber assays have been used to measure fork progression in these studies and nearly all have shown that Rif1 mutants have a slight increase in replication fork progression, although not always statistically significant.
evidence: This is a summary of previous studies.

claim: Rif1-mediated control of replication fork progression could be an evolutionarily conserved function of Rif1.
source: Our observations, taken together with these previous studies, leave open the possibility that Rif1-mediated control of replication fork progression could be an evolutionarily conserved function of Rif1.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the current findings and previous studies.

claim: Rif1 could be recruited to replication forks at a specific time in S phase, or in specific developmental contexts, to modulate the progression of replication forks and provide an additional layer of regulation of the DNA replication program.
source: We do not suggest that Rif1 is constitutively associated with replication forks in all cell types. Rather, Rif1 could be recruited to replication forks at a specific time in S phase, or in specific developmental contexts, to modulate the progression of replication forks and provide an additional layer of regulation of the DNA replication program.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader implications of the findings.
